newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai orders halt to widespread proxy share buying.
newsitem.headline: Dubai orders halt to widespread proxy share buying.

text.p: United Arab Emirates member Dubai has ordered a crackdown on proxy share buying after discovering widespread violations in the share issue of the newly constituted real estate company Emaar Properties.

The official WAM news agency said late on Sunday that Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, who is also UAE's defence minister, had called for measures to curb proxy purchases in new issues in the UAE market.
"Some investors used more than 10,000 names to buy into Emaar Properties," WAM said.
The Emaar issue began on April 2 and closed on April 15. Subscribers could apply for a minimum of 500 shares, at a par value of 10 dirhams, and a maximum of 2.7 million shares.

The state-owned Emirates News daily said on Monday: "The move comes in light of the overwhelming investor response to the initial public offering of (the) newly-constituted company Emaar ...in which many cases of proxy buying have been detected."

The paper described proxy purchases as "buying in the name of other UAE nationals by using their identity cards to ensure that they are allotted (a) maximum number of shares". The subscription was only open to UAE nationals.
The paper made no mention of reports that non-UAE citizens were using proxies to obtain Emaar shares.
WAM quoted Sheikh Mohammed as saying the irregularities could lead to the concentration of shares in the hands of a few big investors.
He said this practice also denied small investors with limited savings the opportunity to make profits on the stock market, and undermined the market's credibility.
Sheikh Mohammed ordered the founding committee of Emaar to maintain the founders' share in the company at 34.3 percent and distribute the remaining 65.7 percent to subscribers.
The firm was initially floated with share capital of 540 million dirhams ($147 million) which was increased to one billion dirhams on order of the Dubai government.
